extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students and researchers in combinatorics and discrete mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and describes criteria, assumptions, and methodological guides for producing and evaluating combinatorial proofs (determinant/lattice-path methods, Cayley's formula proofs, partition identities, Latin-square completion). Useful for writing or checking combinatorial arguments and enumerative proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma aesthetic and applicability criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: What makes a mathematical statement a true Lemma: (1) it should be applicable to a wide variety of instances, even seemingly unrelated problems; (2) the statement should, once you have seen it, be completely obvious; (3) on an aesthetic level, the Lemma — including its proof — should be beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three desiderata when judging or formulating lemmas: broad applicability, immediate obviousness in hindsight, and an aesthetically pleasing/concise proof. Examples referenced: Fatou's Lemma (analysis), Gauss's Lemma (number theory), Burnside–Frobenius Lemma (combinatorics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gessel–Viennot Lemma — applicability and statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Let G = (V,E) be a finite weighted acyclic directed graph, A = {A1,...,An} and B = {B1,...,Bn} two n-sets of vertices, and M the path matrix from A to B with mij = sum_{P:Ai→Bj} w(P). Then det M = sum_{P vertex-disjoint path system} sign P · w(P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To apply the lemma you must (a) have a finite directed acyclic graph (no directed cycles), (b) have edge weights and define path weight multiplicatively (w(P)=product of edge weights; w(path of length 0)=1), (c) form the path matrix whose (i,j)-entry sums weights of all directed Ai→Bj paths, (d) consider path systems given by a permutation σ and n paths Ai→Bσ(i), and (e) restrict to vertex-disjoint path systems — those are exactly the summands of det M. The lemma generalizes the permutation expansion of determinants from bipartite to arbitrary acyclic graphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sign-reversing involution to cancel non-vertex-disjoint path systems
rubrics_metrics.description: In the proof of the Gessel–Viennot Lemma, all non-vertex-disjoint path systems cancel because there is an involution π : N → N (on the set N of non-vertex-disjoint systems) without fixed points such that w(πP)=w(P) and sign πP = −sign P, hence sum_{P∈N} sign P w(P)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the involution by: take minimal i0 whose path intersects another, let X be the first intersection vertex on Pi0, let j0 > i0 be minimal index whose path contains X; swap tails after X between Pi0 and Pj0 to get πP. Show π^2 = identity, weight preserved (same edges), and sign flips because permutation is multiplied by transposition (i0,j0). This is a model technique: design a fixed-point-free, sign-reversing involution that preserves weights to cancel unwanted contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipe: interpret a matrix as a path matrix to relate determinants to enumerative counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret the entries mij of a matrix as path-count weights in a directed (often lattice) graph so that det M becomes a signed weighted sum over vertex-disjoint path systems; with appropriate setup this turns the determinant into an (unsigned) count of combinatorial objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical steps: (1) construct a directed acyclic weighted graph so that each matrix entry equals the total weight (or number) of paths from a designated Ai to Bj; (2) form the path matrix; (3) apply the Gessel–Viennot Lemma to translate det M into a sum over vertex-disjoint path systems; (4) analyze possible permutations/path-systems to evaluate or count them. Use this recipe to obtain combinatorial interpretations (e.g., determinants of Pascal-submatrices count vertex-disjoint lattice path systems, giving nonnegativity and zero/nonzero criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Binet–Cauchy theorem (matrix minor expansion) and graph concatenation interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: If P is an (r × s)-matrix and Q an (s × r)-matrix with r ≤ s, then det(PQ) = sum_{Z} (det P_Z)(det Q_Z), where sum runs over r-subsets Z of columns/rows; combinatorially, in concatenated path graphs, M = PQ and vertex-disjoint path systems from A to C correspond to pairs of systems from A to Z and Z to C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Binet–Cauchy when analyzing concatenation of bipartite path-graphs: represent P as paths from A to B and Q as paths from B to C; the path matrix from A to C factorizes as PQ; conclude that vertex-disjoint systems factor through intermediate column-sets Z and sum over minors. Track permutation signs multiplicatively: sign(στ)=(sign σ)(sign τ). This provides a powerful combinatorial identity for determinants built from concatenated graphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lattice-path interpretation of binomial coefficients and determinant nonnegativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret binomial coefficient (a choose b) as the number of north/east lattice paths from (0,−a) to (b,−b). Placing Ai at (0,−ai) and Bj at (bj,−bj) makes the matrix M with mij = binom(ai, bj) exactly the path matrix for the directed lattice graph; then det M equals the number of vertex-disjoint path systems from A to B, hence is nonnegative and equals 0 iff ai < bi for some i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate determinants of Pascal-submatrices: (1) embed rows/columns at appropriate lattice coordinates; (2) note that each entry counts monotone lattice paths; (3) apply Gessel–Viennot to deduce det M = # vertex-disjoint path systems which is a nonnegative integer; (4) analyze permutations to determine when only identity contributes (e.g., if ai and bj are increasing, only identity permutation is possible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approaches to proving Cayley's formula (acceptable proof types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several distinct valid proof methods for T_n = n^{n−2}: bijection (Prüfer or Joyal style), linear-algebra (matrix-tree theorem/Kirchhoff), recursion (Riordan–Rényi recurrence on forests T_{n,k}), and double-counting (Pitman's refining-sequence argument).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each method has its own structural requirements: bijection proofs must give an explicit invertible mapping and its inverse; linear-algebra proofs must set up incidence/oriented matrices and use determinant identities (Binet–Cauchy, matrix-tree theorem) to count spanning trees; recursion requires correct combinatorial decomposition and induction; double-counting needs two natural enumerations of the same set (e.g., rooted forests vs. refining sequences). Use the method best suited to the intended audience and available tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joyal/Prüfer bijection proof criteria (bijection method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a bijection between labeled trees with two distinguished vertices and all functions from N to N (so |T_n|*n^2 = n^n), by representing a function f:N→N as a directed graph (each vertex has outdegree 1), extracting cycles M, ordering cycle-preimages to choose left/right ends, and building a tree by connecting cycle images as a path and inserting remaining components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To validate a bijection: (1) define the forward map explicitly (graph construction, extraction of cycles, ordering, building t), (2) give an explicit inverse (recover path P between distinguished vertices to obtain M and reconstruct f), and (3) check that mapping is one-to-one and onto. Provide illustrative examples showing both directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix-tree theorem prerequisites and determinant characterization of spanning trees
rubrics_metrics.description: For a connected simple graph G with incidence matrix B (rows vertices, columns edges), orient edges to get C, set M = C C^T (symmetric n×n with degrees on diagonal). Then number of spanning trees t(G) equals det M_{ii} (any cofactor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof steps: apply Binet–Cauchy to expand det M_{ii} as sum over (n−1)×(n−1) submatrices N of Cow i; show det N = ±1 iff corresponding selected edges form a tree spanning all vertices (else det N = 0 by row-dependence). For K_n compute M_{ii} explicitly to obtain n^{n−2}. When applying, ensure consistent orientation (replacing one 1 by −1 in each column) and justify sign/±1 determinants by triangularization via leaf-stripping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursive counting via T_{n,k} and induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Define T_{n,k} as the number of labeled forests on {1,...,n} consisting of k trees with a fixed k-set A occupying distinct components. Establish combinatorial recurrence T_{n,k} = sum_{i=0}^{n−k} binom(n−k,i) T_{n−1,k−1+i} (accounting for neighbors of vertex 1), then solve by induction to obtain T_{n,k} = k n^{n−k−1}. In particular T_n = n^{n−2}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key steps: (1) partition by degree i of a distinguished vertex, (2) count choices of neighbors, (3) reduce to smaller n with adjusted k, (4) apply induction and simplify binomial sums carefully (combinatorial identities/manipulations). State base cases (T_{0,0}=1, T_{n,0}=0 for n>0) and verify boundary conditions (T_{n,n}=1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-counting via rooted forests and refining sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider rooted forests Fn,k (k rooted trees). For fixed F_k denote by N(F_k) number of rooted trees containing F_k, and N^*(F_k) number of refining sequences ending at F_k. Count N^*(F_k) two ways: starting from a tree gives N^*(F_k)=N(F_k)(k−1)!; starting from F_k and inserting edges gives N^*(F_k)=n^{k−1}(k−1)!. Equate to obtain N(F_k)=n^{k−1}, deduce |F_{n,1}|=n^{n−1} and hence T_n=n^{n−2}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define refining sequences clearly (F1⊇F2⊇...⊇Fk with Fi∈Fn,i). Justify counts of ways to add/delete edges: when enlarging F_k to F_{k−1} there are n(k−1) choices for the added directed edge, etc. Use factorial factors to account for orderings of edge deletions/insertions. This is a canonical example of counting the same object in two natural ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generating-function/partition-method: interpret infinite products as partition-generating functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The product ∏_{k≥1} 1/(1−x^k) = ∑_{n≥0} p(n) x^n: interpret factor 1/(1−x^k) as 'allowing any number of parts equal to k' so coefficients count partitions. Other manipulations: ∏_{k≥1} (1+x^k) = ∑ pd(n) x^n (distinct-part partitions), ∏_{i≥1} 1/(1−x^{2i−1}) = ∑ p_o(n) x^n (odd-part partitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using generating functions: (1) map each factor to the combinatorial choice it encodes (presence/multiplicity of part sizes), (2) remove or replace factors to impose restrictions on allowed parts (odd/even/distinct), (3) equate formal power series coefficient-wise to derive combinatorial equalities, ignoring analytic convergence (formal power series context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Glaisher bijection for odd parts ↔ distinct parts (construction and invertibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a partition into odd parts, group equal odd summands and write multiplicities in binary; replace multiplicities by sums of distinct powers of two times that odd summand to obtain a partition into distinct parts. This map is bijective (invertible by collecting parts by largest power of two).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithmic steps: for each odd summand λ_i with multiplicity n_i, write n_i in binary 2^{a1}+2^{a2}+... and replace by parts 2^{a1}λ_i, 2^{a2}λ_i,... . To invert, group parts by odd part when divided by maximal power of 2 and reconstruct multiplicities. Provide small examples to illustrate forward and inverse mappings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler pentagonal theorem bijective approach (Bressoud–Zeilberger involution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal product ∏_{k≥1}(1−x^k) expands as 1 + ∑_{j≥1} (−1)^j (x^{(3j^2−j)/2} + x^{(3j^2+j)/2}). Coefficient sequence c(n) equals 1,−1,0 according to pentagonal numbers. One bijective proof constructs an involution φ mapping partitions from index sets with even j into those with odd j, using a two-case rule depending on t+3j vs λ1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate product identity into convolution condition ∑_{k=0}^n c(k) p(n−k)=0 for n≥1, set explicit candidate c(k) values at pentagonal numbers, and provide the involutive combinatorial map φ: given λ in P(n−b(j)), if t+3j ≥ λ1 produce one transformed partition (case 1), else produce another (case 2); show φ toggles parity of j (maps to P(n−b(j±1))). Verify φ is an involution and that contributions cancel as required. Use worked examples to demonstrate mapping behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracking part-count parity via generating functions (Ed(n)−Od(n) identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce an auxiliary variable y in ∏_{k≥1} (1 + y x^k) to track number of distinct parts; setting y=−1 yields ∏_{k≥1} (1 − x^k) = ∑_{n≥0} (E_d(n) − O_d(n)) x^n, where E_d(n) and O_d(n) count partitions into even/odd numbers of distinct parts respectively. Comparing with Euler's expansion gives explicit values for E_d(n)−O_d(n) (1,−1,0) at pentagonal numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the extra variable y to record combinatorial statistics (e.g., number of parts mod 2). After algebraic manipulation, specialize y to extract parity-weighted counts and equate coefficients to product expansions; derive combinatorial corollaries like the parity difference formula. Provide sample counts (e.g., Ed(10)=Od(10)=5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and necessary condition for completing partial Latin squares
rubrics_metrics.description: A partial Latin square of order n is an n×n array with some cells filled by numbers 1..n so that every number appears at most once in every row and column. To have a chance of completion to a full Latin square one must at least satisfy this row/column at-most-once condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative constructive facts: (a) if first n−1 rows are filled consistently, the last row can always be completed by placing each symbol under the column it's missing from; (b) if only first row is filled, one can complete by cyclically rotating entries in subsequent rows; (c) existence is not guaranteed even when only n cells are filled (explicit counterexample shown). These are necessary but not sufficient conditions; further global constraints (e.g., Hall-type obstructions) may prevent completion.
